title: Void particle retro game made in ~10 hours
author: Bledike
selftext:
Not a big “wow” game. I made it because I played something similar when I was a kid. The goal was to capture that retro feeling and min-max my token usage after I finished my last big project.

I used Claude Fable for game design and the network plan, and Opus 5 for coding and testing (nothing interesting). 

angular, three js + peer js (webRTC)

U can try out, if u want: [https://void-particle.com](https://void-particle.com)

comments.author: _kony2012
comments.body: This is really well-done. I love this. What was the similar one you played when you were a kid? (I assume you don't just mean asteroid but something more like this.)

replies.author: Bledike
replies.body: It’s really hard to say, because it was like 20 years ago. I mostly just remember the feeling of playing local co-op with my friend, sharing one keyboard, but I don't know the game name.

comments.author: IAgreeGames
comments.body: What did you build this on? I love the visual look of it and am interested how you made it!

replies.author: Bledike
replies.body:
I've been developing for 14 years, BUT about 90% of that has been business software, so I don't really have much 3D experience. I've had a couple of projects over the years where I had to do small 3D-related things, but I definitely wouldn't consider myself an expert.

What I *can* describe pretty accurately is how I iterated with AI to get the look.

I had a pretty clear idea of what I wanted to see, both in terms of the UI and the 3D style, so I described it to the AI in roughly 30–40 lines. From that, I had it create a game design document. We then went through about 3–4 iterations discussing how the UI, the game itself, and the gameplay should look and work.

After that, I had it create a POC (proof of concept) using the technologies I'd already chosen. From there, we basically iterated directly on the POC, while continuously updating the design document, until I got the result I was looking for. The whole process took around 2 hours.

One thing I've learned from working with AI (Claude in particular, although I suspect this applies to others too) is that it's surprisingly difficult for it to switch styles, especially once there's already a lot of code written. So I always explicitly told it: if necessary, throw away the entire existing code and rewrite it. The goal is to get the best result, not to preserve the existing code.

So I think the biggest factor was actually having a pretty clear idea of what I wanted before starting the iterations.

replies.author: IAgreeGames
replies.body: That's a good tip for prompting new things, tell it too throw away and start fresh. I've also had good results with adding at the end of things "think outside the box" for ideas and such

comments.author: sw3d
comments.body:
Looks nice man! Love the bullet bouncing off walls and overall aesthetic. Is multiplayer purely WebRTC between peers, or is there a central server? Do you have a Discord for coordinating games?

I've been working on something really similar but in the style of a massive arena: [https://spaceships.gg](https://spaceships.gg) check it out :)

replies.author: Bledike
replies.body:
Yeah, your game is pretty similar too :) GG man!

It’s purely WebRTC, using a shard init seed, a fixed simulation, and its own random number generator. Only the user input is broadcast between the peers.

I actually had a big game project for a kid that I finished, so I wanted a new project to min-max my tokens on. I made this one mostly for fun, so I don’t really have any plans for it beyond that.

replies.author: sw3d
replies.body: Thanks for the details. Id love to try out webRTC for another project, wonder how many peers it could scale to without needing a server (currently my lobbies for spaceships are 32 player max)

replies.author: Bledike
replies.body:
I don't think this P2P approach scales well. Right now (in my game) every client runs the same deterministic simulation at a fixed 60 Hz in lockstep, so a tick only advances once everyone's input for it has arrived, so one slow machine drags the whole match down to its pace.   
  
For larger scale you'd want an authoritative host: one machine runs the simulation (maybe the lobby leader) and broadcasts state (instead of inputs), so a slow client only hurts itself. But that's more network traffic, and the host has to simulate everything and send it to everyone.

replies.author: sw3d
replies.body: Right - currently using the authoritative host for spaceships (60Hz, WASM sim) with event and snapshot relay. It does even up using a lot of resources on the server so I'm wondering if there's a hybrid approach

replies.author: Bledike
replies.body: Hard to tell :) I mostly use Rest API, GraphQL and WebSockets in my work. But I'm pretty sure that if I wanted to build something like this, I'd first try to find a complete solution.

replies.author: Bledike
replies.body: With Angular 21 and signals, Angular can perform just as well as React. I have also been working with Angular in production for around 12 years.
